Empirical Research Plan:  “The Causal Effect of Class Size on Primary-School Achievement in Israel”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy Regression-discontinuity design (RDD) with multiple, equally spaced cut-offs that produce a fuzzy first stage.  
Why appropriate  • The Maimonides rule creates pre-announced discontinuities in actual class size at enrollment values of 41, 81, 121, … pupils per grade.  
• Enrollment itself is not manipulable at the individual-pupil level on either side of the cut-off, so grades that straddle a threshold should be comparable in all respects except class size.  
• Because the jump in class size is less than one-for-one (some non-compliers), the design is “fuzzy.” We therefore estimate the causal effect of class size using a two-stage least squares (2SLS) RDD: first-stage discontinuity → instrument for class size; reduced-form discontinuity → effect on scores; Wald ratio → LATE.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
Treatment variable Actual average class size in a given school–grade cell.

Instrument / running variable  
 • Running variable: total enrollment in that grade, E.  
 • Cut-offs: ck = 40k + 1 (i.e., 41, 81, 121, …).  
 • Instrument (Z): indicator that enrollment is strictly above the nearest lower multiple of 40: Z = 1{E > 40k}. This variable jumps from 0 to 1 at each ck, causing a discrete drop in class size.

Treatment group (locally) Grades with enrollment just above a threshold (Z = 1).  
Control group (locally) Grades with enrollment just below the threshold (Z = 0).  
Timing Cross-sectional; the “event” is contemporaneous with the test year.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes In the absence of treatment, mean test scores would evolve smoothly in enrollment; no other school input changes discretely at ck. Plausible because only class splitting is mandated mechanically.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable Schools cannot finely tune grade enrollment to be just below 40, 80, etc. Plausible: enrollment depends on cohort size and residential patterns, not easily adjusted at the single-pupil margin.

A3. First-stage relevance and monotonicity Crossing ck always (weakly) reduces class size; the sign is known and there are no “defiers.” Holds by construction of the rule.

A4. Local independence of covariates Observable (and unobservable) student and school characteristics change smoothly at ck. Reasonable but testable with covariate balance checks.

A5. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) A grade’s class size change does not spill over to nearby grades in ways that affect their test scores and feed back. Largely plausible because grade-specific resources are quasi-fixed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
T1. Manipulation / sorting around the cut-off  
 • Test with McCrary density test.  
 • Replicate with alternative running variables (e.g., beginning-of-year vs. end-of-year counts).  
 • Show robustness to excluding schools with enrollment exactly at 40, 80, 120.

T2. Discrete changes in peer composition or tracking when a class is split  
 • Check continuity of observable peer characteristics (share disadvantaged, gender mix, parental education).  
 • Control for these covariates in robustness specifications.  
 • Demonstrate that any composition jumps are too small to explain achievement jumps.

T3. Heterogeneous bandwidth sensitivity / functional-form dependence  
 • Report estimates for multiple bandwidth selectors (Imbens-Kalyanaraman, Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik).  
 • Use local linear vs. quadratic fits.  
 • Implement donut RDD dropping ±1 student around each cut-off.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
```r
#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)     # fast data manipulation
library(fixest)         # fast 2SLS with clustering
library(rdrobust)       # RDD inference
library(ggplot2)

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and prepare data
dat <- fread("israel_classsize.csv")  # one row = school–grade

# Key variables already: enrollment, class_size, math_score, read_score
# Create running variable centered at nearest lower multiple of 40
dat[, cutoff   := floor((enrollment-1)/40)*40]        # 0,40,80,...
dat[, dist     := enrollment - cutoff - 40]           # normalised: -39,...,+?
dat[, treat_Z  := as.integer(dist >= 1)]              # 1 just above threshold
# Bandwidth in absolute pupils
bw <- 10
sample <- dat[abs(dist) <= bw]

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Main 2SLS (local linear) pooled over all cutoffs
feols(math_score ~ 1 + class_size | 0 | 
         ~ treat_Z + dist + I(dist*treat_Z) | school_id, 
       data = sample, cluster = ~school_id)

# Alternative straightforward 2SLS with fixest explicit first stage
iv_main <- feols(math_score ~ 1 + dist + I(dist*treat_Z) | 
                   class_size ~ treat_Z + dist + I(dist*treat_Z), 
                 data = sample, cluster = ~school_id)

summary(iv_main)

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Reduced-form & first-stage for diagnostic plots
rf  <- feols(math_score  ~ treat_Z + dist,        data = sample)
fs  <- feols(class_size  ~ treat_Z + dist,        data = sample)

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. McCrary density test
mcr <- rddensity(sample$enrollment %% 40, c = 0)
summary(mcr)

#--------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: different bandwidth & polynomial order
for (b in c(7, 15, 20)) {
  tmp <- sample[abs(dist) <= b]
  mod <- feols(read_score ~ dist | 
                 class_size ~ treat_Z + dist, 
               data = tmp, cluster = ~school_id, degree = 2)
  print(b); print(summary(mod)$coeftable["class_size",])
}
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
Economic theory (and prior empirical work) suggests that smaller classes improve learning, especially in early grades. I expect a negative coefficient: each additional student lowers scores. Magnitude: roughly −0.02 σ in test scores per extra pupil, implying that cutting class size from 40 to 30 (~¼ reduction) would raise achievement by about 0.2 σ.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)

C1 – No manipulation of running variable 1  
C2 – Continuity of covariates at cut-off 1  
C3 – Correct functional form / bandwidth choice 0.5 (needs robustness)  
C4 – Strong first stage (relevance) 1  
C5 – No other discontinuous policies at cut-off 0.5 (possible peer-mix jumps)  

Overall: 4 / 5 conditions clearly satisfied; remaining issues addressed via robustness.
